client: I've been feeling completely stretched thin lately, like no matter what I do, I'm failing somewhere. I'm a nurse working long shifts, and then I come home to two little kids who need everything from me while my partner is overseas. I honestly don't know if talking about it is going to change anything, because the situation is just... it is what it is, you know?
therapist: What you're carrying right now is genuinely enormous — the weight of caring for others around the clock, at work and at home, with your partner so far away. I notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's a kind of quiet exhaustion underneath your words, like part of you has already had to make peace with just pushing through. I'm wondering — when you say "it is what it is," does that feel like acceptance, or more like something you've had to tell yourself just to keep going?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, it's more the second thing — something I tell myself just to keep going. If I actually stopped and let myself feel how hard it is, I think I'd fall apart, and I can't afford to do that when the kids are depending on me and I've got patients who need me to show up. So "it is what it is" is kind of like... armor, I guess.
therapist: That word "armor" is really powerful — it tells me you haven't lost touch with how hard this actually is, you've just had to build a way to survive it. There's so much strength in what you're doing, and also a real cost to never letting yourself put that armor down, even for a moment. I'm curious — is there anywhere in your life right now, even a small pocket of time or a person, where you feel like you *can* set it down, even briefly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, not really — and that's a lonely thing to admit out loud. My closest friend moved away last year, and my partner and I do talk when we can, but there's this gap where I feel like I can't fully unload on him because he's dealing with his own stress being overseas and I don't want to make things harder for him. So I kind of just... hold it all, and by the time the kids are in bed I'm too exhausted to even know what I feel anymore.
therapist: What you just said — "by the time the kids are in bed I'm too exhausted to even know what I feel anymore" — that really stays with me, because it sounds like the exhaustion has become a kind of numbness too. I noticed as you were talking there was something almost hurried in how you said it, like even naming this loneliness felt like something to get through quickly rather than sit with. I wonder if part of you finds it a little scary to slow down and actually let this land — what comes up for you when you imagine really letting yourself feel how isolated you've been?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, it is scary — if I'm being honest, I think I'm afraid that if I really let myself feel it, I'll realize just how alone I actually am, and I don't know what I'd do with that. Like, what's the point of feeling it fully if nothing about the situation changes — my partner is still overseas, my friend is still gone, I'm still walking into that hospital tomorrow. It almost feels self-indulgent to sit in it when I have so much I have to keep doing.
therapist: The word "self-indulgent" really catches my attention — because you'd never say that a patient in pain was being self-indulgent for acknowledging their pain, and yet you're holding yourself to a completely different standard. Feeling something fully isn't the same as being swallowed by it, and in CBT we actually find that when we allow emotions some space, they tend to lose a little of their power to frighten us — it's the *avoiding* them that often keeps them so overwhelming. What do you think that belief — that feeling it is self-indulgent — has cost you over time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That comparison to a patient actually hit me harder than I expected, because you're right — I would never say that to someone I was caring for. But I think what it's cost me is... I don't even really know who I am outside of being useful to people anymore, like somewhere along the way I stopped mattering to myself. And I'm not sure I know how to change that without feeling like I'm stealing time or energy from someone who actually needs it more than I do.
therapist: What you just said — that you've stopped mattering to yourself — that's one of the most important things you could have named, and it took real courage to say it out loud. I want to gently push back on that framing of "stealing" — because the version of you that has nothing left, that's running on empty, isn't actually more available to your kids or your patients, she's just more depleted. What might it look like to start thinking of caring for yourself not as taking from others, but as part of what makes it possible to keep showing up for them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and logically it makes sense — like the whole oxygen mask on a plane thing — but knowing it intellectually and actually believing it are two very different things for me. When I try to imagine carving out time for myself, I immediately think of all the things that would fall through the cracks, like who's going to make sure the kids have lunches packed or that I've followed up on my patients. I guess I'm not sure how to make that shift feel real rather than just like a nice idea that doesn't survive contact with my actual life.
therapist: You're naming something really real — there's often a gap between understanding something and *living* it, and that gap isn't a flaw in you, it's just how deeply these patterns have taken root. I also notice you're speaking very quickly right now, like even imagining space for yourself brings up an urgency to justify why it won't work — which tells me that inner critic moves fast to shut the idea down before it can take hold. What if, instead of imagining a big shift, we got really small — is there even one five-minute thing that used to feel like *you*, before all of this, that we could think about together?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I used to really love sitting outside with a cup of tea in the mornings, just for a few minutes before the day started — nothing special, but it felt like mine. But even as I say that, I'm already thinking that the kids are usually up before me and the mornings are chaos, so it's not like I can just... do that. I don't want to set myself up for something that's just going to feel like another thing I'm failing at.
therapist: Something struck me just then — when you described that cup of tea outside, there was a moment of something that sounded almost like warmth, like a small light coming on, before your words quickly moved to shut it down. I wonder if part of you actually *lit up* a little at that memory, even as another part rushed in immediately to protect you from hoping for it. What if the goal wasn't to perfectly recreate that morning ritual, but just to notice that there's still a "you" in there who knows what she loves — and that's actually a really important thing to have found today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I did light up a little — and then immediately felt almost embarrassed by it, like it was naive to even want something that small. I think you're right that there's still a "me" in there somewhere, and honestly that's both a relief and kind of painful to acknowledge, because it means I've been aware of losing her and just kept going anyway. I'm not sure what to do with that yet, but it feels like something.
therapist: "It feels like something" — I want you to hold onto that, because that's not nothing, that's actually the beginning of something real. The fact that finding her again feels both relieving *and* painful makes complete sense — grief and hope often arrive together, and you've been carrying the quiet loss of yourself for a long time. You don't have to know what to do with it yet; just being willing to acknowledge she's still there, and that she matters, is already a meaningful step.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think part of me came in here expecting to just vent and leave feeling the same, and instead I'm sitting with something I didn't anticipate — which is a little unsettling, honestly. I'm not used to someone reflecting things back to me like that without me having to be okay at the end of it, and I don't quite know what to do when there isn't a tidy resolution. But I think I needed to hear that she still matters, even if I don't fully believe it yet.
therapist: What you just described — coming in to vent and leaving with something unexpected — that's actually what real work feels like, and it makes sense that it's unsettling when you're so used to having to wrap things up neatly for everyone else. I notice you said you don't *fully* believe it yet, and I want to say that "yet" is doing a lot of important work in that sentence — you don't have to believe it completely today. Would you be willing to carry just that one small thing with you this week — not as a task to complete, but just as something to let sit: that she still matters?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think I can try to carry that — it feels less threatening when you frame it as something to let sit rather than something I have to fix or act on. My worry is that the week is going to get loud again really fast, with the shifts and the kids, and that small thing will just get buried under everything else. But maybe that's okay, maybe it doesn't have to survive the whole week perfectly to still mean something.
therapist: What you just said at the end there is actually really wise — "it doesn't have to survive the whole week perfectly to still mean something" — and I wonder if you can hear how different that sounds from the voice that called feeling things "self-indulgent" at the start of our conversation. You're already holding something a little more gently than you were an hour ago, and that matters even if the week gets loud and messy. And if it does get buried, it's not lost — you can always come back and find it again, just like you found her today.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
